p: Picking a neighbor's grain by hand was allowed. Doing it on the Sabbath looked like reaping and threshing.
b: The Law let a hungry traveler pick heads of grain by hand from a neighbor's field, as long as he did not use a sickle (Deuteronomy 23:25). The question here is the day. The Mishnah, written down about AD 200 but drawing on older Pharisaic teaching, lists thirty-nine kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath, among them reaping, threshing and winnowing (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2). Only Luke adds that the disciples rubbed the heads in their hands, which separates grain from husk: a small act of threshing. The Torah itself only says that even in plowing and harvest time Israel must rest (Exodus 34:21). How far that reached was argued among Jewish teachers, and E. P. Sanders points out that the dispute here is of a kind Jews had among themselves.

p: Luke says "some of the Pharisees." His Pharisees are mixed: critics here, hosts and protectors elsewhere.
b: Mark 2:24 has "the Pharisees"; Luke narrows it to "some." The care fits his picture of them across Luke and Acts. Pharisees question Jesus here and in 5:21, but they also invite him to dinner (7:36; 11:37; 14:1), warn him that Herod wants to kill him (13:31), and in Acts the Pharisee Gamaliel defends the apostles (Acts 5:34–39) and believing Pharisees join the church (Acts 15:5). Paul calls himself a Pharisee (Acts 23:6). Readers who take every Pharisee in the Gospels as a hypocrite miss Luke's nuance. The Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to keeping the Law carefully in daily life, and many ordinary Jews respected them.

p: Jesus points to 1 Samuel 21, where David, hungry and on the run, was given the holy bread.
b: In 1 Samuel 21:1–6 David comes to the priest Ahimelech at Nob and asks for food. "The only bread on hand was the Presence Bread" (1 Samuel 21:6), and the priest gives it to him once he hears that the men have kept themselves from women. Jesus argues from scriptural precedent: if Scripture does not condemn David for eating what was reserved for priests when he was in need, his hungry followers are not to be condemned either. The story does not say it happened on a Sabbath, though later Jewish tradition placed it there because the bread was changed on the Sabbath (Leviticus 24:8). Luke, like Matthew, leaves out Mark's mention of Abiathar as high priest (Mark 2:26), a name that does not match 1 Samuel, which has Ahimelech.

p: Greek "the loaves of the setting-out": twelve loaves set before the LORD each Sabbath. The KJV says "shewbread."
b: The Greek hoi artoi tēs protheseōs, "the loaves of the setting-out," is the Septuagint's name for the Hebrew lechem happanim, "bread of the face (presence)." Twelve loaves were set in two rows on a gold table in the holy place, replaced every Sabbath, and eaten only by the priests in a holy place (Leviticus 24:5–9). The KJV's "shewbread" comes from Tyndale and Luther's Schaubrot, "show-bread." This site uses "the Presence Bread" in every book.
orig: οἱ ἄρτοι τῆς προθέσεως (hoi artoi tēs protheseōs)

p: Luke ends on the claim itself, without Mark's saying that the Sabbath was made for human beings (Mark 2:27).
b: Mark gives a reason before the claim: the Sabbath came into being for human beings (Mark 2:27). Matthew adds that priests work in the temple on the Sabbath and that "something greater than the temple" is here (Matthew 12:5–6). Luke has neither, so the story rests wholly on who Jesus is. Readers take "Son of Man" in two ways here. Most see Jesus' own title, from Daniel 7:13, so that he claims authority to say how God's day is kept. A minority, noting that in Aramaic "son of man" can mean simply "a human being," read Mark 2:27–28 as "human beings are lords of the Sabbath"; Luke's wording, without Mark's 2:27, leans toward the title. Neither reading has Jesus abolishing the Sabbath: he keeps going to synagogue on it (4:16; 6:6).

t: The right hand, and "Luke the physician"
p: Only Luke says it was the right hand, the hand for work. Is this a doctor's eye?
b: Mark and Matthew say only "a hand." Luke's "right" hand tells the reader the man had lost the use of his working hand: his living was at stake. Luke adds such details elsewhere too (the right ear, 22:50; a "high fever," 4:38). In 1882 W. K. Hobart argued that this kind of language showed the author was a physician, matching Colossians 4:14. Henry Cadbury answered in 1919–1920 that the same "medical" words are common in educated Greek writers like Josephus and Lucian who were not doctors. Most scholars accept Cadbury's point: Luke's language fits a doctor but does not prove one. The authorship question belongs to the book's opening pages.

a: keeping a close eye on him
t: Was healing allowed on the Sabbath?
p: Jewish teachers agreed that saving a life overrode the Sabbath. A withered hand was not an emergency.
b: The verb paratēreō means watching closely in order to catch someone out (also 14:1; 20:20). Behind the scene is a real legal question. Jewish teaching held that danger to life sets aside the Sabbath (Mishnah Yoma 8:6; the Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 85a–b, gathers arguments for it). A man with a long-withered hand was in no danger, so healing could wait a day (compare 13:14). Jesus' answer in 6:9 refuses the line between emergency and non-emergency: to leave good undone when it can be done is itself a choice for harm. This was an argument within Judaism about how to keep God's day, not an attack on the Sabbath.

a: To save a life, or to destroy it?
p: Greek psychē: life, soul, person. Jesus puts it starkly: not to save is to destroy.
b: The word psychē means a person's life, and in other places the soul or self (9:24; 12:20). Jesus does not ask whether healing is "work." He asks what the Sabbath is for, and puts the alternatives so that there is no neutral middle. Mark has "to kill" (Mark 3:4), and the Byzantine text of Luke has the same, while the oldest manuscripts of Luke read "to destroy" (apolesai). There may be irony in the question: his questioners are already looking for a way to bring a charge against him (6:7, 11).
orig: ψυχὴν σῶσαι ἢ ἀπολέσαι (psychēn sōsai ē apolesai)

p: Greek anoia: mindlessness, folly. Luke has no plot to kill Jesus here, unlike Mark 3:6.
b: Anoia is literally "lack of mind": folly, or rage that has lost its reason (2 Timothy 3:9 uses it for folly). Luke's ending is milder than Mark's, where the Pharisees go out at once with the Herodians to plan how to destroy Jesus (Mark 3:6; Matthew 12:14 is similar). Here they only discuss "what they might do." Luke saves the plot against Jesus' life for Jerusalem (19:47; 22:2), and keeps the Galilean Pharisees as opponents in debate, not yet as plotters.

p: Luke shows Jesus praying before every turning point. The Greek is unusual: "in the prayer of God."
b: Only Luke says Jesus spent the night praying before he chose the Twelve. Luke shows him praying at his baptism (3:21), alone in the wilderness (5:16), before Peter's confession (9:18), at the transfiguration (9:28–29), before teaching the Lord's Prayer (11:1), on the Mount of Olives (22:41–44) and on the cross (23:34, 46). In Acts the church likewise prays before choosing leaders (Acts 1:24; 6:6; 13:3). The phrase en tē proseuchē tou theou is odd Greek. Most take it as "prayer to God"; a few suggested "in the place of prayer of God," since proseuchē can mean a prayer house (Acts 16:13), but on a mountain at night that is unlikely.
orig: ἐν τῇ προσευχῇ τοῦ θεοῦ (en tē proseuchē tou theou)

p: Greek apostolos, "one sent." Luke uses the word far more than Matthew or Mark.
b: An apostolos is someone sent with authority, an envoy. Matthew uses the word once (Matthew 10:2) and Mark perhaps twice (Mark 6:30; 3:14 in some manuscripts), but Luke six times and Acts twenty-eight. For Luke "the apostles" are the Twelve, the witnesses who were with Jesus from John's baptism to the ascension (Acts 1:21–22); in Acts only 14:4 and 14:14 use the word for Paul and Barnabas. The number twelve recalls Israel's twelve tribes (22:30), and Acts 1 fills the place left by Judas so that the number is whole again.

a: to whom he also gave the name Peter
p: Luke has already called him "Simon Peter" (5:8). Here the naming is noted, without Matthew 16's explanation.
b: Peter's Greek name, Petros, means "rock"; John gives the Aramaic Kephas (John 1:42). Mark also records the naming in his list of the Twelve (Mark 3:16). Only Matthew gives Jesus' explanation, "on this rock I will build my church" (Matthew 16:18), where the questions about Peter's role are discussed. Luke names Peter first in every list and gives him a special role at the supper (22:31–32), and he leads the church in Acts 1–12.

p: Mark and Matthew say "the Cananaean," from Aramaic for "zealous." Was he a revolutionary?
b: Luke translates what Mark left in Aramaic: Kananaios (Mark 3:18; Matthew 10:4) comes from qan'ana, "zealous," and Luke writes the Greek zēlōtēs (also Acts 1:13). The word can mean someone zealous for God's Law, like Phinehas (Numbers 25:11) or Paul before he believed (Acts 22:3; Galatians 1:14). It can also name the Zealots, the party that fought Rome. Josephus first calls a faction "the Zealots" during the Jewish War of AD 66–70 (Jewish War 4.160–161), so many historians think Simon was zealous for the Law rather than a member of a later party. Either way, the Twelve put a man of fierce zeal beside Matthew, whom Matthew 9:9 identifies with the tax collector Luke calls Levi (5:27).
r: Mark 3:18; Matthew 10:4; Acts 1:13; Numbers 25:11; Acts 22:3; Galatians 1:14; Matthew 9:9; 5:27

p: The Greek says only "Judas of James." The KJV made him James's brother; most versions say son.
b: Greek often names a man by his father in the genitive ("James of Alphaeus" is "son of Alphaeus"), so most translations read "Judas son of James" here and in Acts 1:13. The KJV's "brother of James" links him with the Jude of Jude 1:1, who calls himself "brother of James," but there the word "brother" is written out. Mark and Matthew have no Judas in this place; they name Thaddaeus (Mark 3:18; Matthew 10:3). Since early times readers have taken Thaddaeus and Judas son of James as one man with two names, and John 14:22 mentions "Judas, not the Iscariot." Others think the lists simply preserve different traditions about the less-known members of the Twelve.

p: Luke's word is prodotēs, a traitor, not Mark's "the one who handed him over."
b: Mark 3:19 and Matthew 10:4 call Judas "the one who also handed him over" (paradidōmi, the verb used for God handing Jesus over too). Luke uses the blunt noun prodotēs, "traitor," a word Stephen later turns on his hearers (Acts 7:52). The verb egeneto, "became," matters: Luke does not say Judas was chosen as a traitor, but that he became one, and later that Satan entered him (22:3).

t: On the mountain or on the plain?
p: Matthew's sermon is on a mountain (Matthew 5:1). Luke's is on level ground, after Jesus comes down.
b: This is why Luke's sermon is called the Sermon on the Plain English Translation. Many readers think a level place on a hillside fits both accounts. Others think each writer shaped the setting: Matthew, with Moses on Sinai in mind, puts Jesus on a mountain to give his teaching; Luke has him meet God on the mountain at night (6:12) and then come down to the people, much as Moses came down from Sinai to the Israelites. On a more critical view, both sermons come from one collection of sayings (Q) that each Gospel set in its own scene, and Luke's shorter sermon is closer to its original length. Either way, Luke places the sermon among the crowds with their sick, not apart from them.

a: the coast around Tyre and Sidon
p: Tyre and Sidon were Phoenician, mostly Gentile cities. Their people are among the listeners.
b: The crowd comes from Judea and Jerusalem in the south and from the Phoenician coast in the northwest, outside the land of Israel. Luke does not say the people from the coast were Gentiles, and Jews lived there too, but the mention points ahead to the good news reaching the nations (2:32; 24:47). Jesus has just recalled Elijah's mission to a widow in Sidon's territory (4:26), and he will say that Tyre and Sidon would have repented had they seen his works (10:13–14). Luke has no visit by Jesus to Tyre, unlike Mark 7:24–31.

a: power was going out of him
p: Luke speaks of Jesus' healing as power (dynamis) flowing from him. The woman in 8:46 feels it too.
b: Luke links Jesus' healings with the Holy Spirit's power. He returns to Galilee "In the Spirit's power" (4:14), "The Lord's power was there for him to heal" (5:17), and when a woman touches his cloak he knows "that power had gone out of me" (8:46, as in Mark 5:30). In Acts the same power comes to the disciples (Acts 1:8), and people seek even Peter's shadow and Paul's handkerchiefs for healing (Acts 5:15; 19:12). Luke does not describe the power as magic: it is God's, given to Jesus by the Spirit (Acts 10:38).

t: The poor, or the poor in spirit?
p: Matthew 5:3 has "poor in spirit." Luke has simply "the poor." Which did Jesus say, and what did he mean?
b: Most scholars think Luke's shorter form, "the poor" (ptōchoi, the destitute, beggars), is closer to the earliest wording, and that Matthew's "in spirit" draws out a meaning already present in Israel's Scriptures, where the poor are also the humble who trust God (Isaiah 61:1; Psalm 34:6). Luke means real poverty: the next lines speak of hunger and tears, and the woes speak of the rich and well fed (6:24–25). This matches his whole book: Mary's song (1:52–53), Jesus' first sermon (4:18), the rich man and Lazarus (16:19–31). Readers still differ on how far Luke's blessing is about economic poverty itself and how far about God's poor, the faithful who have nothing to lean on but God. See the card on this chapter's page.

a: the kingdom of God is yours
p: Luke's blessings speak to the hearers directly: "yours," "you will be given your fill." Matthew's speak of "them."
b: Each blessing in Luke starts like a general saying ("Blessed are the poor") and ends with "you": "the kingdom of God is yours," "you will laugh." Matthew's are in the third person throughout ("theirs," "they will be comforted"). Luke's form reads like a direct announcement to the disciples Jesus is looking at (6:20), and it is matched by four woes, also in the second person, which Matthew does not have. The blessings are not commands to become poor; they declare God's verdict on people in that state, as the prophets did (Isaiah 61:1–3).

p: Luke's "now" sets present need against God's coming reversal, the theme of Mary's song.
b: Only Luke adds "now" to the hungry and the weeping, and again to the full and the laughing in the woes (6:25). The present is turned upside down by what God will do. Mary sang it first: "The hungry he has loaded with good things" (1:53), echoing Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:5–8). Abraham says the same to the rich man: "you got your good things in full during your life" (16:25). Matthew's form, "hungry and thirsty for righteousness" (Matthew 5:6), moves the hunger inward; Luke keeps it in the stomach.

a: toss out your name as something evil
t: Shut out and named as evil
p: Being "cut off" may mean exclusion from synagogue or community. The words are general enough for many settings.
b: Two phrases go beyond Matthew 5:11: "cut you off" (aphorizō, separate, exclude) and "toss out your name as something evil." Some scholars see here the experience of Luke's own readers, Jewish believers excluded from synagogues, which John's Gospel also reflects (John 9:22; 16:2). Others note that the words fit any shunning by family or town, and that Acts shows believers rejected both by some synagogues and by Gentile crowds (Acts 13:50; 16:19–24; 19:9). The claim that a formal synagogue curse on Christians already existed in Jesus' or Luke's day is not supported by early evidence. "Because of the Son of Man" makes loyalty to Jesus the cause.
orig: ἀφορίσωσιν ... ἐκβάλωσιν τὸ ὄνομα ὑμῶν ὡς πονηρόν
r: Matthew 5:11; John 9:22; John 16:2; Acts 13:50; Acts 19:9; 1 Peter 4:14

p: The verb skirtaō is the one used of John leaping in Elizabeth's womb (1:41, 44).
b: Luke uses skirtaō, to leap or skip, only here and in 1:41, 44, where the unborn John leaps for joy when Mary arrives. The word recalls Malachi 4:2, where those who fear God go out "leaping like calves" in the Greek. The joy of the persecuted is the same joy that greeted the coming of the Messiah.

a: Their fathers did the very same things to the prophets
p: The rejected prophet is an Israelite theme, voiced by Israel's own prophets. It is not a charge against Jews as such.
b: Israel's Scriptures themselves confess that the ancestors killed or rejected prophets (Nehemiah 9:26; 2 Chronicles 36:15–16; Jeremiah 26:20–23). Luke takes up this inner-Jewish tradition often (11:47–51; 13:33–34; Acts 7:52). Jesus speaks as a Jew to Jews, and his disciples, all Jewish, are the ones who will suffer like the prophets. Later Christian readers sometimes used these words to brand the Jewish people as prophet-killers; that use takes a self-critical prophetic theme and turns it into an accusation against outsiders. The "fathers" in 6:26 who praised false prophets show that Jesus' point is about how God's people of every age treat God's messengers.

a: your comfort is already paid to you in full
p: Apechō was the word on Greek receipts: "received in full." The rich have had their comfort; there is no more to come.
b: Greek business papyri from Egypt use apechō on receipts to mean "I have received in full," as Adolf Deissmann showed. Matthew uses the word three times of the hypocrites who are "already paid in full" by human praise (Matthew 6:2, 5, 16). Here the rich have their "comfort" (paraklēsis), the word behind "the comforting of Israel" that Simeon waited for (2:25). Abraham's words to the rich man make the same point (16:25). The woes, like the prophets' (Isaiah 5:8–23; Amos 6:1), are warnings that call for change, not curses that settle anyone's fate (compare Zacchaeus, 19:8–9).
orig: ἀπέχετε τὴν παράκλησιν ὑμῶν (apechete tēn paraklēsin hymōn)
r: Matthew 6:2; Matthew 6:5; Matthew 6:16; 2:25; 16:25; 19:8–9; Isaiah 5:8–23; Amos 6:1; James 5:1–5

a: woe to you who are rich
p: The Epistle of Enoch, a Jewish writing older than Luke, has strings of woes against the rich.
b: "Woe" (ouai) is the cry of a funeral lament, used by the prophets against injustice (Isaiah 5:8–22; Habakkuk 2:6–19). The closest parallel to Luke's woes is the last part of 1 Enoch (chapters 94–105, probably second century BC), which pronounces woe after woe on rich oppressors and promises reversal to the righteous poor: "Woe to you rich! You have trusted in your wealth" (1 Enoch 94:8). 1 Enoch is Scripture only in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, but it shows that Jesus' woes spoke in a form his hearers knew. James 5:1–6 uses the same tradition.

p: The false prophets of old were popular because they told people what they wanted to hear.
b: Israel's false prophets promised peace when there was no peace (Jeremiah 6:14; Jeremiah 8:11), and the people loved it (Jeremiah 5:31). Micah mocks the people's favorite preacher, one who prophesies about wine and beer (Micah 2:11). Universal praise is therefore not a mark of a true messenger of God. The last blessing (6:22–23) and the last woe mirror each other: hated like the prophets, or praised like the false prophets.

p: In Luke this is the sermon's first command, straight after the woes. Christians have read it in very different ways.
b: The present imperatives mean ongoing practice: keep loving, keep doing good. Enemies here include persecutors (6:22) and the man who strikes or robs (6:29). Luke's reasons are God's own kindness to the ungrateful (6:35) and what makes disciples different from "sinners" (6:32–34). How these commands apply to war, policing and self-defense divides Christians: the historic peace churches read them as binding on every believer in every setting, while most churches distinguish personal revenge from the duties of rulers. That question has its card at Matthew 5:38–48, on the topic page for nonviolence. Luke's own emphasis is practical: blessing, praying, giving and lending.
r: Matthew 5:38–48; Romans 12:14–21; 1 Peter 3:9; 23:34; Acts 7:60; Proverbs 25:21–22; Exodus 23:4–5

a: When someone hits you on the cheek
p: Matthew has a slap on the right cheek and a lawsuit. Luke has a blow and a robbery.
b: Matthew 5:39–40 specifies the right cheek, which most read as a backhanded insult, and a lawsuit over the tunic, after which one gives up the outer robe too. Luke drops "right" and reverses the order of the garments: someone grabs the outer robe (himation), the cloak worn on top, and the disciple does not hinder him from taking the tunic (chitōn) worn underneath. That is street robbery, not a court case. The scene is a picture, not a legal rule: it describes a person so free from the need to protect themselves that they meet violence with open hands.

p: Jewish teachers and Greek moralists had the rule in its negative form. Jesus gives it positively.
b: The book of Tobit, which is Scripture for Catholics and the Orthodox, says, "Do not do to anyone what you hate" (Tobit 4:15). The Babylonian Talmud tells that Hillel, asked to teach the whole Torah standing on one foot, said: "What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor; that is the whole Torah, the rest is commentary" (Shabbat 31a). Greek and Chinese moralists also knew the rule (Isocrates, Confucius' Analects 15.24). The positive form asks more: not only to refrain from harm but to do the good one would want. In Luke the rule stands in the middle of the love of enemies, so "people" includes enemies too. Matthew places it near the end of his sermon (Matthew 7:12).

a: what thanks do you have coming for that
p: The Greek word is charis: grace, favor, thanks. Matthew's version has "reward."
b: Literally, "what kind of grace (charis) is that to you?" In everyday Greek charis was the favor given or the gratitude owed in return, the glue of patronage and friendship. Luke's repeated question asks what is special, worth thanks, in doing what everyone does. The Plain English Translation's "what thanks do you have coming" leaves open whose thanks: other people's, or God's favor, which Luke calls "reward" in 6:35. Matthew 5:46 has "what reward," and Luke has "reward" in 6:35. In Greek and Roman society, gifts and loans created obligations; Jesus tells his followers to give where no return is possible, which turns the system on its head (14:12–14).
orig: ποία ὑμῖν χάρις ἐστίν (poia hymin charis estin)

p: The Law told Israelites to lend to the poor freely, without interest, even near the year of release.
b: In Galilee's farming villages, a loan of seed or money could keep a family on its land. The Law commanded generous lending to a poor fellow Israelite without interest (Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:35–37) and warned against refusing a loan because the seventh year, when debts were released, was near (Deuteronomy 15:7–11). By Jesus' day the teacher Hillel had created the prozbul, a court document that kept loans from being cancelled in that year, because people had stopped lending (Mishnah Sheviit 10:3–4). Jesus goes beyond the Law's generosity: lend even to enemies, without counting on getting it back. In the Latin Vulgate, 6:35 reads mutuum date, nihil inde sperantes, "lend, hoping for nothing from it," and that line became the medieval church's chief proof text against any profit on a loan: Pope Urban III's decretal Consuluit (about 1186–1187) rests the ban on it, and Benedict XIV's Vix pervenit (1745) restated the ban. Luther read the verse as a command to lend freely to the needy; Calvin's letter on usury (1545) argued that it forbids exploiting the poor, not every interest-bearing loan between parties in business. How the churches weigh interest today is set out on the card at Psalm 15:5, which covers Luke 6:35 as well.
r: Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:35–37; Deuteronomy 15:1–11; Psalm 37:26; Matthew 5:42; 6:35; Psalm 15:5; Proverbs 28:8

p: Children resemble their father. God is kind to the ungrateful, so his children are too. Jesus himself is "Son of the Most High" (1:32).
b: "The Most High" (Hypsistos) is a favorite title of God in Luke (1:32, 35, 76; 8:28; Acts 7:48; 16:17). The angel calls Jesus "Son of the Most High" (1:32), and here those who love enemies become "sons of the Most High": they share his family likeness. Sirach, Scripture for Catholics and the Orthodox, has a close saying: be like a father to orphans, "and you will be like a son of the Most High" (Sirach 4:10). "Sons" is the Greek; Luke's point includes daughters as well.

p: Matthew 5:48 says "perfect." Luke says oiktirmōn, compassionate, a word used of God in the Psalms.
b: Where Matthew has "be perfect (teleioi), the way your heavenly Father is perfect," Luke has oiktirmones, "compassionate," the Septuagint's word for the LORD who is "compassionate and gracious" (Exodus 34:6; Psalm 103:8). Both echo Leviticus 19:2, "You will be holy, because I am holy." An Aramaic paraphrase of Leviticus read in synagogues, Targum Pseudo-Jonathan, has a close parallel at Leviticus 22:28: as our Father is merciful in heaven, so you must be merciful on earth. That Targum reached its final form centuries after Luke, but the saying shows how naturally Jews spoke of imitating God's mercy.

a: Release, and you will be released
p: Luke's verb here is apolyō, "set free, release," not the usual word for forgiving sins.
b: Most English Bibles say "forgive," but the verb is apolyō: to release a prisoner (23:16–25, where Pilate wants to "release" Jesus and releases Barabbas), to send someone away, to free from a debt or charge. In this setting, after "do not condemn," it means letting the accused go free: dropping charges and claims. It overlaps with forgiveness (aphiēmi, 11:4; 17:3–4) but keeps the legal picture. The passive "you will be released" points to God's verdict, as do "you will never be judged" and "you will be given" (6:38). The two prohibitions are worded as in Matthew 7:1, "Do not judge"; Luke's present-tense Greek can also mean "stop judging."

p: A belted robe made a pouch at the chest, used for carrying grain. The measure is pressed, shaken and heaped.
b: The Greek kolpos is the fold of a garment above the belt, where one could carry things (Ruth 3:15 has Ruth hold out her shawl for six measures of barley). A seller who wanted to give good measure pressed the grain down, shook the container so it settled, and filled it until it spilled over. Isaiah 65:6–7 and Psalm 79:12 use the same picture for God paying back "into their lap." The final line is Jesus' rule of measure for measure, also in Matthew 7:2 and Mark 4:24, and a known principle in Jewish teaching (Mishnah Sotah 1:7).

a: Is a blind man able to guide a blind man?
p: Matthew aims this saying at the Pharisees (Matthew 15:14). Luke aims it at the disciples who will teach others.
b: Luke calls a one-line saying a "parable" (parabolē), as the Greek Old Testament calls a proverb a parabolē (1 Samuel 24:13). In Matthew 15:14 Jesus says it about the Pharisees. In Luke it sits between sayings about judging (6:37–42), and so warns disciples: a teacher who cannot see his own faults (6:41–42) will lead his followers into the same ditch. The next verse makes the same point: students become like their teacher.

a: A disciple does not rank above the teacher
p: In Matthew 10:24 the saying warns of persecution. Here it warns that disciples will turn out like those who teach them.
b: The same saying is used in different settings: in Matthew 10:24–25 it means disciples will be treated as their teacher was; in John 13:16 and 15:20 it calls them to serve and to expect hatred. Here it follows the blind guide: a fully equipped (katartizō, made complete, trained) disciple will be like his teacher, faults included. So choose a teacher who sees.

p: A comic picture: a man with a roof beam in his eye offering to remove a speck from his brother's. The rabbis knew it too.
b: Karphos is a speck, chip or bit of straw; dokos is a beam, the main timber of a roof. Jesus' hearers, in a land where most building used stone and timber, would have laughed. The Babylonian Talmud has a similar saying: when a man was told to remove the chip from his eye, he answered, "Remove the beam from your own eyes" (Arakhin 16b), used there of a generation that could not take correction. Whether the saying went from Jesus to the rabbis, the other way, or was a common proverb, we cannot know. Matthew 7:3–5 has it in nearly the same words.

p: Hypokritēs was the Greek word for a stage actor, someone playing a part.
b: In classical Greek a hypokritēs is an actor who answers on stage, and so someone who plays a role. In the Gospels it means a person whose outward show does not match the reality, here a man who corrects others while blind to himself. In Luke Jesus uses the word for the crowds (12:56) and for a synagogue leader (13:15), not only for Pharisees. Here it is aimed at disciples.

a: the good storeroom of his heart
p: Speech shows what the heart has stored up, as fruit shows the tree.
b: The word thēsauros is a treasury or storeroom, the place where valuables are kept and brought out. Matthew has the same image in a debate with the Pharisees (Matthew 12:33–35). Israel's wisdom teachers said the same: guard your heart, for life flows from it (Proverbs 4:23), and Sirach says that as fruit shows how a tree was tended, a person's speech shows the heart (Sirach 27:6). In Luke the sayings about trees and speech follow the warning about teachers, so they help disciples tell good teachers from bad.

p: Calling Jesus "Lord" means little without doing what he says. Matthew's version speaks of the last judgment.
b: Matthew 7:21–23 sets the saying at the judgment, with people who prophesied and drove out demons in Jesus' name being sent away. Luke keeps it in the present: why call me Lord now, and not obey? The doubled address shows urgency or devotion (compare "Master, Master," 8:24). The words lead into the two builders, whose difference is not hearing but doing (6:47–49), a contrast Luke also draws with Jesus' true family (8:21) and with his mother (11:28).

p: Luke's builder digs down to rock. His flood is a river bursting its banks.
b: Matthew contrasts building on bedrock with building on sand, and has rain, floods and winds (Matthew 7:24–27), the flash floods of a Judean wadi. Luke's builder digs, goes deep and lays a foundation (themelios), and the danger is a river (potamos) in flood. Some scholars (Jeremias among them) think Luke adapted the story for readers outside Palestine who built with deep foundations near rivers; others think both versions fit Galilee. The point is the same: storms test every house, and only one built on obedience stands. Israel's Scriptures use the same picture (Proverbs 10:25; Ezekiel 13:10–14).

p: A fishing town on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, Jesus' base in Galilee.
b: Capernaum (Hebrew Kefar Nahum, "Nahum's village") lay on the northwest shore of the lake, near the border between Herod Antipas' Galilee and Philip's territory, which is why it had a customs post (5:27) and soldiers. Excavations by Franciscan archaeologists uncovered a white limestone synagogue of the 300s–400s AD built over the black basalt foundations of an earlier building, which some date to the first century; and a house venerated as Peter's from early times (4:38). Luke has already set teaching and healings there (4:23, 31–41).

p: A centurion commanded about a hundred men. In Antipas' Galilee he was probably in Herod's service, and a Gentile.
b: A centurion (hekatontarchēs) led a company of roughly eighty to a hundred soldiers. Galilee was ruled not by Roman governors but by Herod Antipas, so this officer probably served in Antipas' forces, which were organized on the Roman model and included non-Jews. 7:5 and 7:9 make clear he is a Gentile. Luke speaks well of centurions: one confesses Jesus at the cross (23:47), Cornelius is the first Gentile convert (Acts 10), and Julius treats Paul kindly (Acts 27:1–3, 43).

p: Luke calls him a doulos, a slave. Matthew calls him a pais, a servant or boy. John's similar story has a royal official's son.
b: Luke says doulos (7:2, 3, 10), the ordinary word for a slave, which this site renders "slave" because Greek and Roman slavery was ownership of a person, not hired service. The centurion himself calls him pais (7:7), a word that can mean "servant" or "boy," and Matthew uses pais throughout (Matthew 8:6, 8, 13). Some have read pais as "son," which would bring Matthew close to John 4:46–54, where a royal official in Capernaum asks Jesus to heal his son. Luke's "prized" (entimos, valued, honored) shows real attachment, but he does not soften the fact that the man was owned.

a: he sent some Jewish elders to him
p: In Matthew the centurion speaks to Jesus face to face. In Luke he sends elders and then friends, and never meets Jesus.
b: Matthew 8:5–13 tells the story briefly, with the centurion pleading in person. Luke has two delegations and the centurion never appears. Augustine, harmonizing the Gospels, argued that Matthew speaks of the centurion coming because he came through others, as people say a man does what he does through his agents (Harmony of the Gospels 2.20). Many modern scholars think Luke has expanded the story to show the centurion's humility and his good standing with the Jews, and to prepare for Cornelius, who also sends messengers and is praised by Jews (Acts 10:1–8, 22). Others think Matthew shortened it. Both agree on the center: the centurion's faith in Jesus' word.

a: he built the synagogue for us himself
p: Non-Jews sometimes paid for synagogue buildings. An inscription from Asia Minor honors one such benefactor.
b: Gentile sympathizers who honored Israel's God, called "those who fear God" in Acts (Acts 10:2; 13:16), sometimes gave money for synagogues. An inscription from Acmonia in Phrygia, from the later first century AD, says the synagogue there was built by Julia Severa, a Gentile woman who was also a priestess in the imperial cult. In Galilee a wealthy officer funding the village synagogue would have made him a patron, owed honor and favors in return; that is the elders' argument ("he is worthy"). The centurion himself refuses that claim (7:6–7).

t: A Jew in a Gentile's house
p: Many Jews avoided entering Gentile homes for reasons of purity. The centurion spares Jesus the question.
b: Peter tells Cornelius that a Jew was not supposed to associate with a foreigner or visit him (Acts 10:28), and the Mishnah treats the dwellings of Gentiles as unclean (Mishnah Ohalot 18:7). Practice varied: Jews and Gentiles did business, and how strict people were differed by group and region. The centurion may be respecting Jewish scruples, or simply saying he is not worthy of such a guest. Either way, Jesus never enters his house, and in Acts it takes a vision from God to bring Peter into Cornelius' house (Acts 10:9–29; 11:1–18).

p: The centurion's words became the prayer said before Communion in the Catholic Mass.
b: The Latin Mass has, from early medieval times, a prayer before Communion based on the centurion's words in Matthew 8:8 and here. In English it runs: Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word and my soul shall be healed. The 2011 English Missal restored "under my roof." Anglican and other liturgies have similar prayers of humble access. The word hikanos means "fit, sufficient" ("good enough"), and in 7:7 the centurion uses the verb of worth, axioō. The elders said he was worthy (7:4); he says he is not. John the Baptist used the same word of himself: "I am not good enough to untie the strap of his sandals" (3:16).
orig: οὐ γὰρ ἱκανός εἰμι (ou gar hikanos eimi)

p: The centurion reasons from the army: an officer under orders gives orders, and they are done without his being there.
b: His point is not that he is powerful but that authority works at a distance. He obeys those above him and is obeyed by those below; so Jesus, under God's authority, can command illness with a word. The same words appear in Matthew 8:9, and the Plain English Translation words them the same way. Luke's "placed" (tassomenos, appointed, stationed) stresses that his authority is delegated.

p: Jesus is amazed at a Gentile. Luke leaves out Matthew's saying about many coming from east and west, and uses it later (13:28–29).
b: Only twice do the Gospels say Jesus was amazed: at a Gentile's faith (here and Matthew 8:10) and at his hometown's unbelief (Mark 6:6). Matthew follows this story with the saying that many will come from the east and west to eat with Abraham while "the sons of the kingdom" are thrown out (Matthew 8:11–12); Luke places a form of that saying at 13:28–29. In Luke the story looks ahead to Acts, where Gentiles hear and believe (Acts 10:34–48; 28:28). It does not set the centurion against the Jews: Jewish elders plead for him, and he loves their nation.

p: A village in the Jezreel Valley, near Mount Tabor, across a hill from Shunem, where Elisha raised a widow's son.
b: Nain is mentioned nowhere else in the Bible. It is usually identified with the Arab village of Nein, on the north slope of the Hill of Moreh in the Jezreel Valley, about 20–25 miles (35–40 km) southwest of Capernaum. On the other side of the same hill lies Shunem, where Elisha raised the son of a woman who had shown him hospitality (2 Kings 4:8–37). Luke's readers who knew their Scriptures would hear an echo: the prophet's raising of a mother's only hope, done again nearby.

a: his mother's only son, and she was a widow
p: Losing her only son left a widow with no one to support or protect her.
b: In a world without pensions, a widow depended on her sons. With her husband and her only son dead, this woman had lost her support and her family's future. The Law repeatedly charges Israel to protect widows (Exodus 22:22; Deuteronomy 10:18), and Luke gives widows special attention (2:37; 4:25–26; 18:1–8; 20:47; 21:1–4; Acts 6:1; 9:39). The words echo the widow of Zarephath, whose son Elijah raised (1 Kings 17:17–24), a story Jesus has just recalled (4:25–26). The Greek monogenēs is "only" (also 8:42; 9:38).

a: A good-sized crowd of townspeople was with her
p: Burial came the same day, outside the town, with family, neighbors and mourners walking behind the bier.
b: Jews buried the dead quickly, usually on the day of death, in tombs outside the town. The body, wrapped in cloth, was carried on an open bier, and the town joined the procession; joining a funeral was a deed of kindness. Mourning involved weeping, wailing women and flutes; the Mishnah says even a poor man must provide at least two flutes and one wailing woman for his wife's funeral (Mishnah Ketubot 4:4). Two crowds meet at the gate: the one following Jesus and the one following the dead.

a: the Lord's heart went out to her
p: Here, for the first time in the story of Jesus' ministry, Luke the narrator calls Jesus simply "the Lord."
b: In Luke 1–2 "the Lord" in the narrative is God, while angels and Elizabeth call Jesus Lord (1:43; 2:11). From here on Luke the narrator often calls Jesus ho kyrios (7:19; 10:1, 39, 41; 11:39; 12:42; 13:15; 17:5–6; 18:6; 19:8; 22:61; 24:3), a usage Mark almost never has. It is the title the church used for the risen Jesus (Acts 2:36). The compassion is just as striking: splanchnizomai, to be moved in one's inner parts, which this site renders "his heart went out to." No one asks Jesus to act; he sees the widow and goes to her.

a: laid his hand on the open coffin
p: Contact with the dead made a person unclean. Jesus touches the bier and stops the procession.
b: The soros was an open bier or coffin on which the body lay. Under the Law, touching a corpse made a person unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11–16), and later teaching extended uncleanness to what the dead lay on. Being unclean was not sin; it was a normal condition, removed by washing, but it kept a person from the temple until then. Jesus' touch does not make him unclean in the story; instead, life flows the other way. The same pattern appears with the woman's touch and the dead girl in 8:43–55.

p: Luke repeats the words of 1 Kings 17:23, where Elijah raises the widow's son at Zarephath.
b: In the Greek Old Testament, Elijah "gave him to his mother" (1 Kings 17:23), the same words Luke uses here (edōken auton tē mētri autou). The parallels pile up: a widow, an only son, a town gate (1 Kings 17:10), a prophet. The crowd draws the conclusion at once: "A great prophet has been raised up among us!" Jesus answers John's question in 7:22 with "the dead are raised," and this story stands just before it.

a: A great prophet has been raised up among us
p: The crowd sees a prophet like Elijah, or the prophet like Moses. The verb also means "raised."
b: Moses promised that God would "raise up" a prophet like him (Deuteronomy 18:15), and Acts applies that promise to Jesus (Acts 3:22; 7:37). Many Jews also expected Elijah to return (Malachi 4:5; 9:8, 19). The crowd's verb ēgerthē is the same verb Jesus has just used to the dead man, "get up" (7:14): a prophet has been raised, and so has the young man. Luke shows that "prophet" was a true but not complete answer to who Jesus is (9:18–20; 24:19).

p: The same words close Zechariah's song: God has visited his people (1:68). The verb means to come and look after.
b: The verb episkeptomai means to come and see about someone: to look after, care for, sometimes to judge. In the Greek Old Testament God "visits" his people to rescue them (Genesis 50:24; Exodus 4:31; Ruth 1:6). Zechariah sang that God "has visited his people" (1:68) and that the Dawn from on high will visit us (1:78). The crowd at Nain says it has happened. Later Jesus weeps over Jerusalem because it did not recognize "the season when you were visited" (19:44).

p: Nain is in Galilee, so "Judea" here means the whole land of the Jews, not only the southern region.
b: Luke sometimes uses "Judea" for the whole Jewish homeland, including Galilee (4:44; 23:5; Acts 10:37), as Roman writers did. Here the news spreads through all the land of the Jews and the surrounding regions, and so reaches John the Baptist in prison (7:18).

p: John had announced "the one stronger than I am" who was coming (3:16). Was he doubting, or asking for others' sake?
b: "The Coming One" is not a fixed title in Jewish texts, but it echoes John's own preaching (3:16), Psalm 118:26 ("Blessed is the one who comes"), and the messenger and the Lord who come in Malachi 3:1–2. John is in prison (3:20), and Jesus is healing and eating with sinners rather than bringing the fiery judgment John described (3:9, 17). Many church fathers held that John knew the answer and sent his disciples so they would see for themselves. Most modern readers take the question as honest: even the greatest prophet had to wrestle with a Messiah unlike the one he expected. Jesus answers with deeds and Scripture, not a title.

t: Healing in front of the messengers
p: Only Luke has Jesus heal many people while John's messengers watch.
b: Matthew 11:4 has Jesus tell the messengers to report what they "are hearing and seeing." Luke spells it out: at that very hour Jesus heals the sick and the possessed and gives sight to the blind, so the messengers become eyewitnesses. "Granted the gift of sight" uses charizomai, to give freely, the same verb as the lender who "freely canceled" debts (7:42).

a: the poor are told the good news
p: Jesus answers in Isaiah's words, the same program he read in Nazareth (4:18). A Dead Sea Scroll has a similar list.
b: The list gathers phrases from Isaiah: the blind see and the deaf hear (Isaiah 35:5–6), the dead rise (Isaiah 26:19), good news for the poor (Isaiah 61:1, read in Luke 4:18). Luke has just shown nearly every item: the blind (7:21), skin disease made clean (5:12–16), the dead raised (7:11–17). A fragment from Qumran, the Messianic Apocalypse (4Q521), says that in the days of God's Messiah the Lord will heal the wounded, give life to the dead and bring good news to the poor. It shows that Jews before Jesus linked these signs with the Messiah's time. Jesus leaves out Isaiah's "release to the captives," perhaps tellingly, since John stays in prison.

a: not tripped up because of me
p: Skandalizō: to trip, to stumble, to be put off. Jesus warns John not to fall over the kind of Messiah he is.
b: A skandalon is the trigger of a trap or a stone that trips someone. This site renders the verb "trip up," as in Matthew 11:6. The blessing is gentle but pointed: blessed is the one, even John, who does not stumble over a Messiah who heals and forgives instead of bringing fire at once.

a: A reed that the wind shakes?
t: A reed shaken by the wind
p: Reeds grew along the Jordan. Some scholars think the reed also pointed at Herod Antipas, whose early coins bore a reed.
b: On the surface, John was no flimsy reed bending with every wind: he stood firm, and it put him in prison. Gerd Theissen noted that the first coins Herod Antipas struck for his new city of Tiberias (about AD 19–20) carried a reed, a symbol of the lake region, and suggested that Jesus' hearers would hear a dig at Antipas, the ruler who bent with every wind and lived in the palaces of 7:25. Not every scholar accepts the coin link, but the contrast between John and Antipas' court is plain.

a: 'Look, I am sending my messenger before your face.
p: The quotation blends Malachi 3:1 with Exodus 23:20. It says "your face," not Malachi's "before me."
b: In Malachi 3:1 God says, "I am about to send my messenger, and he will clear a road before me." Exodus 23:20 has God promise Israel an angel (the same Greek word, angelos, "messenger") to go ahead of them on the way. Jesus' wording (the same wording appears in Matthew 11:10 and, as the narrator's quotation, Mark 1:2) joins the two and shifts "before me" to "before your face": the messenger goes ahead of the one God sends. Malachi later names the messenger as Elijah (Malachi 4:5). Luke has already applied Isaiah 40:3 to John (3:4–6); here Jesus himself identifies John as the forerunner.

a: the smallest one in the kingdom of God
p: John is the greatest human being, yet the least in God's kingdom is greater. Readers explain this in several ways.
b: Most take it to contrast two eras: John belongs to the time of promise (16:16) and stands at its threshold; whoever shares in the kingdom Jesus brings has something more, not in personal worth but in privilege. Some church fathers took "the smallest one" (mikroteros, "the lesser") to be Jesus himself, younger than John and thought less of, yet greater; Chrysostom gives this view. A third view asks whether John is excluded from the kingdom; Luke's own answer is no, since all the prophets will be in it (13:28).

a: they declared that God was in the right
t: "Declared that God was in the right"
p: Dikaioō, "justify," with God as object means declaring him in the right. The people did it by accepting John's baptism.
b: The people "justified God": they acknowledged that God was right in sending John and calling them to repent. They did not prove anything; they owned that God was right, and the tax collectors showed it by being baptized. The same verb returns in 7:35, where the passive fits "wisdom is proved right" and later in a darker sense, when people try to "justify themselves" (10:29; 16:15). Whether 7:29–30 are Jesus' words or the narrator's comment is debated. The SBL text sets them in parentheses as the narrator's aside, and many translations agree; others read them as Jesus still speaking. Either way, they show who has responded to God's plan and who has not.

p: Nomikoi, "lawyers," is Luke's usual word for the experts in the Law of Moses. It overlaps with "scribes."
b: Luke uses nomikos six times (7:30; 10:25; 11:45, 46, 52; 14:3), where Mark and Matthew usually say "scribes" (grammateis). The word would be clearer to Gentile readers: these were specialists in interpreting the Law of Moses, not lawyers in a modern court. "God's plan" (boulē) is a key word for Luke: God's will working through history (Acts 2:23; 13:36; 20:27). The refusal of these leaders does not cancel God's plan; it only shuts them out of it "for themselves."
orig: οἱ νομικοί (hoi nomikoi); τὴν βουλὴν τοῦ θεοῦ

a: We piped a tune for you
p: Children in the square call to each other, but nobody plays along with wedding music or with a funeral.
b: Village children played at weddings (dancing to pipes) and funerals (wailing a lament). In this little parable a group complains that the others will not join either game. Most readers take the complaining children as "this generation": they wanted John to dance and Jesus to mourn, and rejected both. Others reverse it: John called them to mourn and Jesus invited them to the feast, and they joined neither. The second fits the order of 7:33–34, John's fasting and Jesus' eating. The point is the same: nothing pleases people who have decided not to respond.

a: He overeats and he is a heavy wine drinker
p: The insult echoes the charge against the rebellious son in Deuteronomy 21:20, a son to be stoned.
b: The words phagos and oinopotēs recall the parents' charge against a stubborn son: "He is a glutton and a drunkard" (Deuteronomy 21:20, where the Greek uses different words of similar meaning). Under that law such a son was to be stoned. Jesus' critics may have meant the echo: a rebel against God's ways. The charge itself shows how much Jesus ate with others, and with whom (5:29–32; 15:1–2; 19:7). Luke's next scene, a dinner with a Pharisee and a woman known as a sinner, shows him doing exactly what he is accused of.

a: wisdom is proved right by all her children
p: Wisdom is God's wisdom, pictured as a woman, as in Proverbs. Her children are those who accept her messengers.
b: In Proverbs, Wisdom is a woman who calls in the streets, builds a house and invites people to her feast (Proverbs 1:20–33; 9:1–6); Wisdom of Solomon says she enters holy souls in every generation and makes them friends of God and prophets (Wisdom of Solomon 7:27). Here John and Jesus are her envoys (compare 11:49), and her "children" are the tax collectors and people who received them (7:29). Matthew 11:19 has "by her works." Luke's "all her children" leads straight into the woman of 7:36–50, one of those children.
r: Proverbs 1:20–33; Proverbs 8:1–36; Proverbs 9:1–6; Wisdom of Solomon 7:27; 11:49; 7:29; Matthew 11:19

p: At formal dinners guests lay on couches, leaning on one elbow, with their feet away from the table.
b: Greek, Roman and well-to-do Jewish banquets were eaten lying on couches around low tables, each guest propped on the left elbow with the feet stretched behind. That is how the woman could stand "behind him, by his feet" without crawling under a table. Large houses had a courtyard or open dining room, and at a feast for a visiting teacher, uninvited villagers might come in to watch and listen. A woman entering was unusual but not impossible.

p: Luke never says what her sin was. That she was a prostitute is an assumption, though a common one.
b: Hamartōlos, "sinner," describes someone known for not living by God's Law: tax collectors, those in shameful trades, people whose way of life was public. "Of that town" suggests her reputation was known locally. Many readers have assumed she was a prostitute, and her loosened hair (7:38) and anointing have been read that way, but the text does not say. Luke also never names her. Later Western tradition identified her with Mary Magdalene (8:2) and with Mary of Bethany; the Gospel gives no ground for either link.

p: All four Gospels tell of a woman anointing Jesus. Luke's story differs in place, time, meaning and characters.
b: In Mark 14:3–9 and Matthew 26:6–13 a woman anoints Jesus' head in Bethany, in the house of Simon the man with skin disease, days before his death, and he calls it a preparation for burial. In John 12:1–8 Mary of Bethany anoints his feet and wipes them with her hair. Luke's story is in Galilee, early in the ministry, at a Pharisee named Simon's house, about forgiveness. Some think there were two events, one in Galilee and one in Bethany, whose details later mixed (the feet and hair in John). Others think one event was told in different forms. Luke has no Bethany anointing in his passion story, perhaps because he had told this one.

p: A respectable woman kept her hair covered or bound in public. Letting it down before men was shocking.
b: In Jewish and Greco-Roman custom, a married woman's unbound hair in public was a mark of indecency or of grief. The Mishnah lists going out with loose hair among things for which a husband could divorce his wife without paying her marriage settlement (Mishnah Ketubot 7:6). The woman uses her hair as a towel, kisses his feet again and again (the verb kataphileō means kissing fondly, repeatedly), and pours costly oil on them. To the host it looks like scandal; to Jesus it is love.

p: Simon thinks a prophet would know who she is. Jesus shows he is a prophet by reading Simon's own thoughts.
b: Simon's silent reasoning has two steps: a prophet would know she is a sinner; a holy man would not let her touch him. Luke's irony is that Jesus answers the thought no one spoke (7:40), so he does know, both the woman and Simon. He also knows what Simon does not: that she has been forgiven. Simon's concern may include purity, but a sinner's touch did not make a person ritually unclean under the Law; his concern is reputation and holiness.

p: Simon was the most common Jewish name of the time. He is probably not the Simon of Mark 14:3.
b: About one Jewish man in ten in this period seems to have been called Simon, to judge from names in tombs and documents, so the Pharisee here need not be Simon "the man with the skin disease" of Bethany (Mark 14:3), though some have equated them. Simon addresses Jesus respectfully as "Teacher" (didaskale), and Jesus treats him as a host worth teaching, not an enemy.

p: A denarius was a day's wage. One man owed about a year and a half's wages, the other about seven weeks'.
b: A denarius was a Roman silver coin, the usual daily pay for a laborer (Matthew 20:2). Five hundred denarii was a crushing debt for a peasant; fifty was serious but manageable. In Aramaic the same word, chova, means "debt" and "sin," which is why the Lord's Prayer can speak of debts (Matthew 6:12) or sins (11:4). The parable turns money into a picture of sin and forgiveness.

p: The verb charizomai comes from charis, "grace": he canceled the debts as a free gift.
b: Greek has many words for canceling a debt; Luke picks charizomai, to give graciously, to forgive freely, from charis, grace. Paul uses it for God forgiving sins (Colossians 2:13). The parable's question, "which will love him more?", sets the order: first the gift, then the love that answers it. That order matters for reading 7:47.

a: you offered me no water for my feet
p: Water for the feet, a kiss and oil were signs of welcome. Was Simon's omission an insult, or only ordinary?
b: Abraham had water brought for his guests' feet (Genesis 18:4), and "You have made my head rich with oil" (Psalm 23:5) pictures a generous host. A kiss of greeting was usual among friends and family. Kenneth Bailey argued that leaving out all three was a deliberate snub before the other guests. Others, among them Amy-Jill Levine, caution that we have little evidence that every host was expected to provide these, and that reading Simon as rude can feed an old habit of making Pharisees look bad. Jesus' point does not depend on either view: what Simon did not do, she did, lavishly.
r: Genesis 18:4; Genesis 24:32; Psalm 23:5; 1 Samuel 25:41; John 13:4–14; Romans 16:16

t: Forgiven because she loved, or loved because forgiven?
p: The Greek "for" (hoti) can give the cause or the evidence. The parable points one way; the sentence alone could go either.
b: Read alone, "her sins have been forgiven, for (hoti) she has loved much" could mean her love earned forgiveness. But the parable just told (7:41–43) runs the other way: the debtor forgiven more loves more. And the next clause says the one forgiven little loves little, not the reverse. So most interpreters, Catholic and Protestant, take her love as the evidence and fruit of a forgiveness she already received, perhaps through John's preaching or an earlier meeting with Jesus. The perfect tense "have been forgiven" (apheōntai) fits that. Older Catholic exegesis often read her love as contrition joined to charity, through which she received forgiveness. See the card on this chapter's page. 7:50 names faith as what saved her.

p: The passive points to God as the one who forgives, as at 5:20. The guests hear Jesus claiming God's prerogative.
b: Jesus speaks the same words he said to the paralyzed man (5:20). The passive leaves God as the forgiver, but Jesus pronounces it with authority, and as at 5:21 the hearers ask what kind of man forgives sins. The repetition after 7:47 makes public, to her face, what Jesus has just told Simon.
orig: ἀφέωνταί σου αἱ ἁμαρτίαι (apheōntai sou hai hamartiai)

p: The same words close healing stories (8:48; 17:19; 18:42). In this story there is no illness: salvation is forgiveness and peace.
b: The verb sōzō means to save, rescue, heal, make whole. This site keeps "saved" in healing stories too, so the link stays visible (8:36, 48, 50). Here no disease is healed, so the meaning is plainly forgiveness and a restored life. "Go in peace" (literally "into peace") is a Hebrew farewell (1 Samuel 1:17) that also sends her into a new state. Faith and love are not rivals in the story: faith brought her to Jesus, love showed what she had received.
orig: ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε (hē pistis sou sesōken se)

a: one town and village after another
p: Luke pictures Jesus on the move with a group: the Twelve and a company of women.
b: Luke likes short summaries that move the story on (4:14–15, 44; 8:1–3). This one gathers the company that will travel with Jesus to Jerusalem: the Twelve, already chosen (6:13–16), and women who support the group. "Preaching and telling the good news of the kingdom of God" sums up his work (4:43). Luke will send out the Twelve to do the same (9:1–6), and then seventy-two others (10:1–12).

p: "Magdalene" means from Magdala, a town on the lake. Nothing in Luke makes her the sinful woman of 7:37.
b: Magdala (Hebrew Migdal, "tower") stood on the west shore of the lake, north of Tiberias; it is probably the town Josephus calls Taricheae, known for salting fish. Excavations from 2009 uncovered a first-century synagogue there with a carved stone showing a menorah. Mary had been freed from seven demons; Luke says nothing about sexual sin. In AD 591 Pope Gregory the Great preached that the sinful woman of 7:37, Mary of Bethany and Mary Magdalene were one woman, and Western art and legend made her the repentant prostitute. The Eastern churches never made that link and honor her as "equal to the apostles." The Catholic calendar separated the figures in 1969, and in 2016 Pope Francis raised her day to a feast, calling her "apostle to the apostles."

p: Seven means fullness: her affliction was severe. Mark's later ending says the same (Mark 16:9).
b: Seven is the Bible's number of completeness. Seven demons mean she was gravely afflicted, perhaps in body and mind, as Jesus' saying about the unclean spirit that returns with "seven other spirits" suggests (11:24–26). The Longer Ending of Mark repeats the detail (Mark 16:9). Nothing in it implies moral failure; Luke lists her among women "cured" of spirits and sicknesses.

a: Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's steward
p: A woman from Herod Antipas' court followed Jesus. She was at the empty tomb (24:10).
b: Chuza was Antipas' epitropos, a steward or estate manager, a high post in the court at Tiberias. Richard Bauckham notes that the name Chuza is attested in Nabatean inscriptions, so he may have come from the Nabatean kingdom. Joanna must have been a woman of means and status. She reappears among the women who found the tomb empty and told the apostles (24:10). Luke may owe some of his knowledge about Herod's court (9:7–9; 13:31; 23:6–12) to her. Bauckham also suggests that she is the Junia whom Paul calls "outstanding among the apostles" (Romans 16:7), Junia being a Latin name that sounds like Joanna; this is a possibility, not a consensus.

p: Diakoneō means to serve: at table, with money, in any ministry. These women paid for the mission out of their own means.
b: The women "served" (diēkonoun) from their possessions (hyparchonta, property, means). The same verb is used for serving at table (4:39; 10:40; 22:26–27) and for the apostles' "service of the word" (Acts 6:2–4), and it gives English "deacon." Here it means they financed the traveling group, as patrons. That women traveled with a teacher was unusual, and many scholars see in Luke a deliberate record of women as disciples who followed Jesus from Galilee to the cross and the tomb (23:49, 55; 24:1–10). How far these texts bear on women's leadership in the church today is debated; see the topic page on women in church leadership.

a: There was a sower who went out to scatter his seed
t: The sower in three Gospels and Thomas
p: Luke's sower is shorter than Mark's. The parable is also in the Gospel of Thomas (saying 9).
b: Luke follows Mark 4:1–20 closely but trims it, and the Plain English Translation opens the parable as Mark 4:3 and Matthew 13:3 do, adding only Luke's "his seed." He sets it among crowds from town after town (8:4), not by the sea in a boat; he adds that the seed by the road was trampled; he has rock instead of rocky ground; and he gives only the hundredfold yield. The Gospel of Thomas, a sayings collection found in Coptic at Nag Hammadi in Egypt and dated by most scholars to the 100s, has a version without the explanation, which some scholars think independent of the Gospels and others think dependent on them. Thomas is in no church's Bible.

p: Mark and Matthew have "rocky patches." Luke has "the rock" and says the plant dried out for lack of moisture.
b: Galilee's limestone often lies just under a thin layer of soil, which Mark describes as "rocky ground" with shallow earth. Luke simply says "rock" (petra), and instead of the sun scorching the shoot he says it had no moisture. Some see Luke's version as more natural to readers who did not know Galilean fields. In the explanation (8:13) the rock stands for people with no root, who fall away in testing.

p: A very rich harvest. Isaac reaped a hundredfold when God blessed him (Genesis 26:12).
b: How exceptional a hundredfold yield was is debated. Joachim Jeremias argued that ordinary yields were around seven- to tenfold, so a hundredfold signaled the miracle of God's harvest; others reply that ancient writers report high yields for single seeds and fertile land. Either way, the hearer is meant to be struck: despite all the losses, the harvest is great. Genesis says Isaac "reaped a hundred times what he sowed" (Genesis 26:12), a sign of the LORD's blessing. Luke gives only the top figure, where Mark and Matthew list thirty, sixty and a hundred.

a: Let anyone who has ears to hear listen.
p: Jesus said these words with a raised voice. Luke's whole section is about hearing well.
b: The verb phōneō means to call out loudly. Luke's chapter turns on hearing: the soils are four kinds of hearers (8:12–15), "watch how you listen" (8:18), and Jesus' true family are those who "hear the word of God and do it" (8:21). The call echoes the Shema, "Hear, O Israel" (Deuteronomy 6:4), and the prophets' charge against ears that do not hear (Jeremiah 5:21; Ezekiel 12:2).

a: the mysteries of the kingdom of God
p: A mystērion is a secret God has decided to reveal, as in Daniel. It is not a puzzle that cannot be understood.
b: In Daniel, God reveals "mysteries" (Aramaic raz, Greek mystērion) about what will happen (Daniel 2:18–19, 28). The Dead Sea Scrolls use raz for God's hidden plan revealed to the faithful. Mark has the singular "the mystery" (Mark 4:11); Luke and Matthew the plural. "You have been given" is a gift: the disciples do not earn insight, they receive it. Paul uses the word for God's plan now made known, including the inclusion of the Gentiles (Romans 16:25–26; Ephesians 3:3–6).
r: Daniel 2:18–19; Daniel 2:28; Mark 4:11; Matthew 13:11; Romans 16:25–26; Ephesians 3:3–6

a: though they look, they may not see
p: Luke gives only a short echo of Isaiah 6:9–10 here. He quotes it in full at the very end of Acts.
b: Mark and Matthew quote or echo Isaiah 6:9–10 more fully at this point, Matthew with a formula of fulfillment (Matthew 13:14–15). Luke keeps only a brief allusion, and leaves out Mark's grim "in case they turn back and are forgiven" (Mark 4:12). He saves the full quotation for Paul's last words in Rome, the closing scene of Luke-Acts (Acts 28:25–28). In Isaiah God tells the prophet to say, "Listen and listen, but do not understand" (Isaiah 6:9). How the "so that" should be read, as purpose or as result, is discussed at Mark 4:12.

p: Luke turns the seed into "the word of God," a phrase he uses often in Luke and Acts for the Christian message.
b: Mark says the sower sows "the message" (ho logos, Mark 4:14). Luke writes "the word of God" (ho logos tou theou), his favorite name for the message about Jesus (5:1; 8:21; 11:28; Acts 4:31; 6:7; 12:24; 13:44). In Acts "the word of God kept growing" (Acts 6:7; 12:24), as if the seed of this parable were still spreading. In the explanation (8:12–15) Luke says simply "the word." Mark 4:14–20 and Matthew 13:19–23 have the same bare Greek, ho logos, and the Plain English Translation renders it "the message" there; in Luke it stays "the word," because Luke has just named it "the word of God" (8:11).
orig: ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ (ho logos tou theou)

a: to keep them from believing and being saved
p: Only Luke says why the devil takes the word away: so they will not believe and be saved.
b: Mark has Satan carry the message off (Mark 4:15) and Matthew "the evil one" (Matthew 13:19); Luke says "the devil" (diabolos, "slanderer"), the name he used in the testing (4:2–13). His added purpose clause uses the vocabulary of the church's preaching: believe and be saved (Acts 16:31; Romans 10:9). Some critics see Luke's own wording here; either way, Luke makes the parable speak to his readers' experience of the gospel.
orig: ἵνα μὴ πιστεύσαντες σωθῶσιν (hina mē pisteusantes sōthōsin)

a: in a season of testing they turn away
p: Luke repeats kairos, "season": believing for a season, falling away in a season of testing.
b: The Greek plays on kairos (time, season): they believe "for a season" (pros kairon) and fall away "in a season of testing" (en kairō peirasmou). Peirasmos means testing or trial: persecution in Mark's version ("hardship or persecution," Mark 4:17), and in Luke any pressure that tests faith (22:28, 40, 46). The verb aphistēmi, "turn away, fall away," is the word from which "apostasy" comes. The Lord's Prayer asks not to be brought into testing (11:4).
orig: ἐν καιρῷ πειρασμοῦ ἀφίστανται (en kairō peirasmou aphistantai)

a: worries and wealth and the pleasures of life
p: Luke adds "pleasures" to Mark's worries and wealth. All three return as warnings later in Luke.
b: Worries (12:22–26; 21:34), wealth (12:13–21; 16:13; 18:22–25) and pleasures (hēdonai) are what choke the word in Luke's world: not persecution but comfortable, busy life. "Bring nothing to ripeness" (telesphoreō, to bring fruit to maturity) means the plant grows but never yields.

p: Kalos kai agathos, "fine and good," was the classic Greek phrase for a noble person. Luke uses it for the good soil.
b: Greek readers would recognize kalos kai agathos, "beautiful and good," the ideal of the cultured gentleman in Greek literature. Luke gives it new content: the noble heart is the one that hears the word, holds it fast and bears fruit "by endurance" (hypomonē, steady perseverance, as in 21:19). Where Mark has hearing and welcoming (Mark 4:20) and Matthew understanding (Matthew 13:23), Luke stresses holding on over time.
orig: ἐν καρδίᾳ καλῇ καὶ ἀγαθῇ (en kardia kalē kai agathē)

p: A small clay oil lamp gave light to a whole room only if it stood high. Luke's version mentions people coming in.
b: Houses were lit by small clay lamps burning olive oil, set on a stand or a ledge. Hiding one under a jar or a bed (a couch on legs) would make lighting it pointless. Matthew 5:15 uses the saying of disciples as light to the world, Mark 4:21 of the hidden kingdom coming to light. Luke uses it here and again at 11:33, and his "so that those coming in may see" may picture a house of the Greek kind, with an entrance hall; some read it as a hint of outsiders coming to faith.

p: Mark says "watch what you are hearing" (Mark 4:24). Luke says "how": the manner of hearing decides the fruit.
b: A small change with a point: the seed is the same for every soil, so what matters is how it is received. The saying that follows, "anyone who has something will be given more," sounds unfair as an economic rule; as a rule of hearing it is simply true: those who hold on to the word receive more, those who do not lose even what they seem to have. Luke's "seems to have" (dokei echein) suggests their hold was never real.
orig: βλέπετε οὖν πῶς ἀκούετε (blepete oun pōs akouete)

p: Luke tells this scene without Mark's earlier note that Jesus' family thought he was out of his mind.
b: In Mark 3:20–21, 31–35 the family comes to take Jesus home because people say he is beside himself, and he points to those around him as his true family. Luke leaves out the hostile setting and places the scene after the parable of the sower, so it reads as an illustration of good hearers. His picture of Mary is positive throughout: she hears the word and believes (1:38, 45), keeps things in her heart (2:19, 51), and is with the believers in Jerusalem (Acts 1:14). Who Jesus' "brothers" were (sons of Mary, of Joseph by an earlier marriage, or cousins) divides the churches; see the card at Mark 6:3.

a: hear the word of God and do it
p: Jesus does not reject his family. He widens it to everyone who hears and does God's word, as Mary did.
b: Luke's form ties the saying to the sower ("hear the word," 8:15) and to the two builders ("listens to my words and acts on them," 6:47). Later a woman blesses Jesus' mother, and he answers that those who hear God's word and keep it are blessed (11:27–28). Many readers, Catholic and Protestant, note that this praises Mary rather than excludes her, since she said "May it be done to me just as you have said" (1:38).

a: the far shore of the lake
p: Mark and Matthew call it "the sea." Luke, who knew the Mediterranean, calls it a lake (limnē).
b: Mark and Matthew follow the Hebrew habit of calling any large body of water a "sea" (yam), hence "the Sea of Galilee." Luke always calls it limnē, "lake" (5:1–2; 8:22–33), the word a Greek geographer would use; at 5:1 he calls it Lake Gennesaret. It is about 13 miles (21 km) long and 8 miles (13 km) wide, lying some 700 feet (210 m) below sea level.

a: A gale of wind swept down onto the lake
p: Cool winds drop from the heights around the lake into its deep basin, raising sudden storms.
b: The lake lies in a deep basin with steep hills and the Golan Heights to the east and Mount Hermon to the north. Cool air pouring down the valleys can whip up violent squalls without warning, which is why Luke says the gale "came down" (katebē) onto the lake. A first-century fishing boat recovered from the mud near Ginosar in 1986, about 27 feet (8.2 m) long, shows the kind of open boat that could be swamped quickly.

p: Epistatēs, "master, chief," is a title only Luke uses, and only disciples and those seeking help use it.
b: Where Mark has "Teacher" (didaskale, Mark 4:38) and Matthew "Lord" (Matthew 8:25), Luke has epistata, a Greek word for an overseer or commander. It occurs only in Luke (5:5; 8:24, 45; 9:33, 49; 17:13), always from disciples or from people asking for mercy. Luke may have chosen it because "rabbi" would mean little to Gentile readers. The doubling ("Master, Master") shows panic.

a: spoke sternly to the wind and the surging water
p: In Israel's Scriptures only God commands the sea. Jesus "rebukes" the storm as he rebuked demons and fever.
b: The verb epitimaō ("speak sternly, rebuke") is the one Jesus used against the demon (4:35) and the fever (4:39). The Psalms praise the LORD who rules the raging sea and stills its waves (Psalm 89:9; Psalm 65:7), and in Psalm 107 sailors cry to the LORD in a storm and "He brought the gale down to a hush" (Psalm 107:29). The story of Jonah, asleep in a ship in a storm, stands behind the scene too (Jonah 1:4–16). The disciples' closing question, "Who can this be?", points to the answer the Psalms give.

p: Luke's question is softer than Mark's "Why are you timid? You still don't have faith?" (Mark 4:40).
b: Luke often handles the disciples more gently than Mark. In Mark they rebuke Jesus ("doesn't it matter to you that we are going down?", Mark 4:38) and he asks if they still have no faith; in Luke they simply cry for help and Jesus asks where their faith has gone, implying they have some but did not use it. Matthew places the rebuke before the calming (Matthew 8:26). Critical scholars see Luke's habit of sparing the Twelve, whom he presents as the future witnesses of Acts; others see different emphases in the tellings of one event.

p: The east side of the lake was largely Gentile country, part of the Decapolis. Here pigs were kept.
b: Luke says the region is "across from Galilee": the eastern shore, outside Antipas' Jewish territory, in lands tied to the Greek cities of the Decapolis. This is Jesus' only visit to Gentile territory in Luke. Which town and which shore are meant is uncertain, because the manuscripts name the region in three ways (see the variant). A Byzantine monastery at Kursi on the eastern shore, near a steep slope, marks the place pilgrims came to honor as the site of the miracle from the 400s on.

a: He stayed among the tombs, not in a house.
p: Tombs, demons, nakedness and pigs: everything here is unclean by the Law. Isaiah 65 has the same cluster.
b: Isaiah describes a rebellious people "who sit among the tombs / and spend the night in hidden places, / who eat the meat of pigs" (Isaiah 65:4), the same combination of tombs and pigs in a land of unclean worship. Tombs carried the uncleanness of death (Numbers 19:16). The man without clothes, outside society and living with the dead, is a picture of total ruin. In 8:35 he is clothed, sitting at Jesus' feet, his mind sound.

p: "The Most High God" is how non-Jews often named Israel's God. The demon knows exactly who Jesus is.
b: Theos hypsistos, "God Most High," is often on the lips of non-Israelites in the Bible, though Abram (Genesis 14:22) and the Psalms (Psalm 57:2; Psalm 78:35, 56) use it too: Melchizedek (Genesis 14:18–20), the Babylonian king (Daniel 3:26; 4:2), and the slave girl with a spirit at Philippi (Acts 16:17). Inscriptions show Gentiles in the Greek world worshipping "the Most High God." On this Gentile shore the demon uses the title, and like the demon in the synagogue (4:34) it knows more than the people do. "What is there between me and you?" is a Semitic way of saying "Leave me alone; we have nothing in common."
orig: υἱὲ τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ὑψίστου (huie tou theou tou hypsistou)

p: A Roman legion had about five thousand soldiers. Some readers hear a protest against Roman occupation.
b: The name says the man is occupied by a multitude. A legion was the largest unit of the Roman army, some five to six thousand men. Several scholars read the story politically: a land occupied by "Legion," with a herd of pigs driven into the sea as Israel's enemies were at the Sea of Reeds. The boar was one of the emblems of the Tenth Legion (Fretensis), but that legion was based in Syria before the war of AD 66 and in Jerusalem after 70, not in the Decapolis; if the pigs carried that hint, it spoke to Mark's and Luke's readers after 70 more than to Jesus' first hearers. Others think this reads too much into the word, which Luke explains simply: many demons had entered him. Both readings agree that Jesus is stronger than whatever possessed the man.

p: The demons fear the abyss, the deep prison of evil spirits. Mark has them ask not to be sent out of the region.
b: In the Greek Old Testament abyssos translates the "deep" of Genesis 1:2 and the depths of the earth (Psalm 71:20). In Jewish writings it became the prison of rebellious spirits (1 Enoch 10:4–6 pictures fallen angels bound in a dark pit until judgment), and in Revelation the pit of the locusts and their king (Revelation 9:1–11), the place from which the beast rises (Revelation 11:7; Revelation 17:8), and where Satan is locked away (Revelation 20:1–3). Luke's demons beg not to be sent there before their time, as Matthew's ask "Did you come here to torment us ahead of time?" (Matthew 8:29). Mark 5:10 has them ask not to be sent out of the region.
r: Genesis 1:2; Psalm 71:20; Romans 10:7; Revelation 9:1–11; Revelation 11:7; Revelation 17:8; Revelation 20:1–3; 1 Enoch 10:4–6; Mark 5:10; Matthew 8:29

p: Pigs were unclean to Jews (Leviticus 11:7) but common among Gentiles. Readers have puzzled over their loss.
b: "The pig ... is unclean for you" (Leviticus 11:7), so a herd of pigs marks this as Gentile land. Why Jesus allowed the demons to enter the pigs has been explained in several ways: to show visibly that the man was freed; to show the destructive aim of the demons, who ruin whatever they enter; or as judgment on an unclean place. Modern readers often ask about the animals and the owners' loss; the text does not address it, and the townspeople's response (8:37) shows they counted the cost. Some read the drowning as the demons' own end in the waters of chaos, ironically the abyss they feared.

p: Sitting at a teacher's feet was the posture of a disciple. The man from the tombs is now a learner.
b: Paul says he was brought up "at the feet of Gamaliel" (Acts 22:3), and Mary, Martha's sister, sits at Jesus' feet listening (10:39). The former madman, now clothed and in his right mind (sōphroneō, to be of sound mind), sits like a disciple. Luke's women of 8:2 and this man show what Jesus' healing is for: a new life of following. The townspeople, seeing it, are afraid.

p: Luke says the man was "saved" (sōzō): delivered and healed. Mark says only what happened to him.
b: Following this site's practice, sōzō is rendered "save" in healing stories, so readers can see that healing and salvation use one word. Luke uses the verb three times in this chapter for physical rescue (8:36, 48, 50) and once for the spiritual sense (8:12). The overlap is deliberate: in Luke salvation is the whole restoration of a person.

a: tell all that God has done for you
p: Jesus says "tell what God has done." The man tells "what Jesus had done." Luke lets the two stand side by side.
b: The shift from God to Jesus in one verse is striking, and Mark has the same pattern ("the Lord," then "Jesus," Mark 5:19–20). Many readers see a deliberate statement: what Jesus did, God did (compare Acts 10:38, "God was with him"). Others note that Jesus himself gives the glory to God, and the man simply tells it as he saw it. Unlike Jairus' family (8:56), this man is told to make the news known: in Gentile territory there was no danger of popular hopes for a political Messiah, and he becomes the first witness there.
