p: The synagogue leader organized the meetings, chose readers and kept order. It was a post of local honor.
b: Luke calls Jairus archōn tēs synagōgēs, "leader of the synagogue," and in 8:49 uses the more usual title archisynagōgos, which this site renders "synagogue leader" (gloss: a local leader who ran the meetings). The Theodotus inscription from first-century Jerusalem records a priest and synagogue leader who built a synagogue "for the reading of the Law and the teaching of the commandments." Jairus was a man of standing; falling at Jesus' feet was a public act of humility.

p: The girl is twelve; the woman has bled for twelve years. The two stories are woven together.
b: Mark and Luke sandwich the woman's healing inside the story of Jairus' daughter. The number twelve links them: the girl has lived twelve years, the woman has suffered twelve years. Twelve was close to the age when a Jewish girl came of age (later rabbinic law set it at twelve and a day), so the girl dies just as her life as a woman would begin. The woman's flow had made her life as a woman a long ordeal. Both are called "daughter" (8:42, 48), and both are "saved" (8:48, 50).

p: Claude's theory: Luke uses the thornbushes' verb, "choke," for the crowd around Jesus. Pressing close is not yet faith.
b: This is Claude's own suggestion. The verb sympnigō, "choke," appears in Luke only twice: for the thornbushes and life's cares that choke the word (8:14), and here for the crowds pressing on Jesus (Mark 5:24 has a different verb, synthlibō). Luke may intend the echo: the whole crowd is jammed against Jesus (8:45), but only one woman touches him with faith and is "saved." Being close to Jesus in the crowd, like hearing the word among thorns, does not of itself bear fruit. Commentators often note the crowd versus the believing touch; the verbal link with 8:14 is less often drawn and may be a coincidence of vocabulary.

a: a flow of blood for twelve years
p: Under Leviticus 15 a long flow of blood made a woman unclean. It did not bar her from daily life or from touching Jesus.
b: "A woman may have a flow of blood for many days" (Leviticus 15:25): such a woman was unclean while it lasted, and what she lay or sat on became unclean too (Leviticus 15:25–27). Impurity mattered mainly for the temple and for holy food. Amy-Jill Levine and others warn against the common sermon claim that she was banned from society or that touching Jesus broke a Jewish law; nothing forbade her to be in a crowd, and Jews did not think touching an unclean person was sin. Her suffering was the illness itself, the cost of treatment, and twelve years of hope deferred. Luke, unlike Mark 5:26, does not say the doctors made her worse.

p: Kraspedon is the tassel the Law commanded on the corners of clothing (Numbers 15:38). Jesus wore them.
b: The Law told Israelites "to make tassels for themselves on the corners of their clothes" (Numbers 15:38) as reminders of God's commands. That Jesus wore them shows him a Torah-observant Jew. Older English Bibles say "hem" or "border," which hides this. A popular sermon claim links the tassel with Malachi 4:2, "healing in its wings" (the Hebrew kanaf means both wing and corner); that is a later reading, not something Luke says.
r: Numbers 15:37–41; Deuteronomy 22:12; Matthew 9:20; Matthew 14:36; Matthew 23:5; Malachi 4:2

p: The woman had wanted to stay hidden. Jesus calls her out, and her healing becomes a public testimony.
b: Why did Jesus insist on knowing who touched him (8:45–46)? Luke's telling answers: she must declare "before all the people" what happened. Her secret healing becomes a public restoration, after twelve years of an illness that kept her on the margins. Jesus then calls her "daughter," a word of belonging. Luke adds that she told the reason she touched him, so the crowd hears her faith in her own words.

p: Luke usually names John before James, perhaps because Peter and John act together in Acts.
b: Mark 5:37 has "Peter, James, and John," the usual order. Luke has "Peter, John and James" here and at the transfiguration (9:28), and in the list of apostles in Acts 1:13. In Acts Peter and John are a pair (Acts 3:1–11; 4:13–19; 8:14), while James is killed early (Acts 12:2). The three see what others do not: the girl raised, the transfiguration (9:28–36).

p: Jesus does not deny she has died (8:53, 55). Sleep is a common biblical picture of death, from which one wakes.
b: The mourners laugh because they know she is dead, and Luke confirms it: "her spirit came back" (8:55). Jesus' word "asleep" (katheudei) speaks of death as God sees it, a sleep from which he will wake her (Daniel 12:2; John 11:11–14; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14; Acts 7:60). A few interpreters have suggested she was in a coma and only seemed dead, but that is not how Luke tells it. Christians who teach "soul sleep" between death and resurrection appeal to this language; most churches read it as a figure of speech for death's temporary hold.

p: Mark gives Jesus' Aramaic words, "Talitha koum." Luke, writing for Greek readers, gives only the Greek.
b: Luke often leaves out Mark's Aramaic expressions (compare Mark 7:34; 14:36; 15:34). Here the Greek "Child, get up" (hē pais, egeire) matches "Young man, I tell you, get up" at Nain (7:14). Luke also drops Mark's note that she walked about (Mark 5:42), and adds that her spirit returned.

p: The phrase recalls Elijah's raising of the widow's son, where the boy's life comes back inside him.
b: In 1 Kings 17:22, "The boy's life came back inside him, and he lived." Luke's "her spirit (pneuma) came back" uses the Greek picture of the life-breath leaving and returning (compare 23:46, where Jesus commits his spirit to the Father). The practical order to give her food shows she is truly alive, as the risen Jesus eats fish to show he is no ghost (24:41–43). These raisings bring people back to ordinary life; they will die again. Luke presents them as signs of the resurrection to come, not the resurrection itself.

a: to tell no one what had taken place
p: The Gerasene man was told to tell everyone (8:39). Jairus' family is told to tell no one. Why?
b: Mark's Gospel often has Jesus command silence, a feature scholars call the "messianic secret" (see the topic on Mark). Luke keeps fewer of these commands, but keeps this one. Explanations include: to avoid crowds seeking only miracles; to prevent a political movement around a wonder-working Messiah in Jewish Galilee; or because the meaning of Jesus' deeds could only be understood after the cross and resurrection (9:21–22). The command could hardly keep a raised girl secret, so most take it as limiting publicity rather than hiding the event.
